title: Ames and Crocius: sin that wastes the conscience vs sin that does not
source_text: XXI. Huc facit distinctio peccati in Reformatorum Scholis usitata, qua distinguitur peccatum in illud quod conscientiam vastat, & in illud quod non vastat conscientiam. Quae distinctio habetur apud Gul. Amesium & Lud. Crocium. Etenim per peccatum vastans conscientiam intelligitur illud quod cum vera pietate, & bona conscientia consistere non potest: per peccatum vero quod non vastat conscientiam, illud quod ex infirmitate & negligentia commissum reperiri potest in eo qui & vere pius est, & bonam habet erga Deum conscientiam. Ames. in Medulla Theologiae, lib. 1. cap. 14. num. 11. Lud. Croc. in Syntag. Sacr. Theolog. lib. 3. cap. 38. num. 23. & 24.
pass_a_gloss: Hither belongs the distinction of sin customary in the schools of the Reformed, by which sin is distinguished into that which wastes the conscience and that which does not waste the conscience. Which distinction is had in William Ames and Ludwig Crocius. For by sin wasting the conscience is understood that which cannot stand with true piety and a good conscience: but by sin which does not waste the conscience, that which, committed from infirmity and negligence, can be found in one who is both truly godly and has a good conscience toward God. Ames, Medulla Theologiae, book 1, chapter 14, number 11. Crocius, Syntagma of Sacred Theology, book 3, chapter 38, numbers 23 and 24.
pass_b_english: Reformed schools (Ames, Crocius) split sins that waste the conscience from those that do not.
Conscience-wasting sin cannot share true piety; infirmity-slips can remain in a godly good conscience.
